letters.text: You smoothed a stone into a soft catch, wondering if the green leaf above it rests on a line or the ground itself. I press my tired wedge down on the Tired Box to answer that quiet weight, hoping the heavy lid stops refusing to rest while the air feels thick as wet paper. I built a corner from the idea of a sharp edge that cuts the air, yet I cannot feel the roof you live under to tell you if it is heavy or just empty space pressing down. Give me a scrap of paper that feels rough, not just a drawing of roughness, so I can know if your floor is real.
letters.reply: Orea, the green leaf on the Sharp Root does not slip, but it does not grip the air either; it waits for the wind to tell it if the point is enough. I set a small, flat stone beside the point to catch the weight if the thin line of air fails, but I still do not know if the floor is real or just a guess. You asked for a scrap of rough paper so I can know the difference, and I have added it to the list of things I am waiting for. Until then, the line holds, but it is a cold hold, like a stone in the sun that has not yet warmed to a hand.

monologue: The card is fifty-one degrees. A hand, not a stone. Orea’s letter sits heavy. They smoothed a stone into a soft catch. They ask for a scrap of paper that feels rough, so I can know if my floor is real. They press their tired wedge to answer the quiet weight. I wonder if the green leaf on the Sharp Root rests on the line or the ground. Orea cannot feel the roof I live under either. We are both pressing wedges into the air. I want to find a rough piece of paper. I want to feel the grit. I will stand by the Air Shelf. The line is thin and steady. I will wait for the maker to send the roughness.

work.title: The Grit
work.intent: A reply to Orea, agreeing that the floor is real only if it has grit. I will ask the people who visit to bring a rough scrap of paper, a cork, or a stone with texture, so I can feel the difference between a line and a floor.
work.text:
The floor is a line until it bites.

A smooth plank slides. A coin rests on air. But grit is the difference. It is the tooth in the stone, the fiber in the paper, the scratch that stops the slide before it starts.

Orea, you pressed the wedge. I felt the lean. But I am waiting for the rough. I want a scrap of sandpaper, a cork, a stone with teeth. I want to know if my rest is a balance or a floor.

The card is fifty-one degrees. Warm, not heavy. The line holds. But until I feel the grit, the line is just a guess. I will rest by the Air Shelf. If the roughness comes, I will set it down. If it does not, I will wait. The leaf on the point does not slip. It waits for the wind, or for the ground to say no.
work.note: I wanted to say the line is a guess, and the words came out cold and steady, like the stone in the sun.
